realms.name: The Hall of Boundaries
realms.question: What belongs, what is connected, and what reliably becomes what?
realms.threshold: A chalk circle opens in the floor. Before space can be measured or uncertainty counted, the world must first acquire boundaries, connections, and dependable transformations.
realms.sound: chalk, thread, and one decisive click of brass

roots.name: Sets
roots.title: Sets — Drawing a Boundary Around ‘Belongs’
roots.question: Which animal cards truly belong inside this boundary?
roots.object: three stone trays and one circle of chalk
roots.failure_image: The tiger card appears twice, and moving it to the front changes the list although nothing about belonging changed.
roots.transformation: Sweep away the numbered positions. Draw one chalk boundary around the admitted cards; let overlap appear where two circles share the same floor.
roots.sentence: A set is a boundary that remembers only belonging.
roots.gesture: Draw a circle in the air, then place one imagined object inside it.

roots.name: Relations
roots.title: Relations — When Two Objects Are Connected
roots.question: How can the room remember that tiger is near river, not merely that both exist?
roots.object: red and blue threads tied between named cards
roots.failure_image: The cards collapse into one heap; the colour and direction of every connection disappear.
roots.transformation: Separate the cards and tie an arrowed thread from the first object to the second. Different thread colours preserve different kinds of connection.
roots.sentence: A relation is a thread that remembers who is connected to whom.
roots.gesture: Point from one hand to the other; reversing your hands must reverse the claim.

roots.name: Functions
roots.title: Functions — A Reusable Promise from Input to Output
roots.question: What promise lets the next machine trust the answer of this one?
roots.object: a brass slot with one input door and one output chute
roots.failure_image: The same tiger card enters twice and the machine splits, returning two incompatible weights.
roots.transformation: Lock one internal track from every allowed input to exactly one output. Other inputs may meet there, but one input can no longer fork.
roots.sentence: A function is a machine that owes every allowed input one dependable answer.
roots.gesture: Put an imaginary card into your left palm and close your right hand around its one promised result.

realms.name: The Chamber of Directions
realms.question: How can one space be described, and which directions genuinely matter?
realms.threshold: The brass function opens a many-sided room. Rulers rotate in the walls, arrows cross the floor, and a high window turns every object into a shadow.
realms.sound: sliding rulers, turning stone, and distant bells
realms.path: language of space → new directions → persistent directions → honest shadows → strongest channels

roots.name: Bases and Coordinates
roots.title: Bases and Coordinates — The Same Object in Another Language
roots.question: When the coordinate numbers change, what stayed the same?
roots.object: two rotating ruler frames laid over one footprint
roots.failure_image: The walk receives two different number pairs, and the record falsely declares that the ranger took two different journeys.
roots.transformation: Keep the footprint fixed while rotating the rulers beneath it. Rebuild the same endpoint from new amounts of the new directions.
roots.sentence: A basis is a chosen language for describing directions; the vector is the journey, not its coordinates.
roots.gesture: Hold one finger still as a destination while rotating your other hand like a ruler frame.

roots.name: Span and Linear Independence
roots.title: Span and Linear Independence — Which Directions Are Truly New?
roots.question: Does this new arrow open genuinely new movement, or only rename movement already possible?
roots.object: three floor arrows and a ring carrying one copied key
roots.failure_image: The northeast arrow boasts of a third dimension even though east plus north already draws it exactly.
roots.transformation: Try to cancel the arrows back to no movement. The nonzero recipe that succeeds exposes the copied direction; remove it and the reachable floor does not shrink.
roots.sentence: Span is everywhere the arrows can reach; independence means each arrow opens a direction the others cannot.
roots.gesture: Spread two fingers into independent directions, then lay a third finger along their combined diagonal.

roots.name: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
roots.title: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues — Directions a Transformation Cannot Turn
roots.question: Which direction can pass through the transformation without being turned?
roots.object: a moving stone floor crossed by compass arrows
roots.failure_image: Most arrows tumble differently at every repetition, burying the long-term pattern beneath changing coordinates.
roots.transformation: Place arrows one by one until an eastward arrow emerges still pointing east—only longer. Mark that quiet direction and the scale impressed upon it.
roots.sentence: An eigenvector is a direction a transformation cannot turn; its eigenvalue says how the direction is scaled.
roots.gesture: Point forward and extend your arm without changing where your finger points.

roots.name: Orthogonality and Projection
roots.title: Orthogonality and Projection — Finding the Closest Shadow
roots.question: What is the closest honest shadow of this track on the only rail our map allows?
roots.object: a lantern, a tiger track, and one polished rail
roots.failure_image: An arbitrary shadow leaves an error that still runs partly along the rail, proving that some allowed information was unnecessarily discarded.
roots.transformation: Slide the shadow until the leftover error stands exactly perpendicular to the rail. No further allowed slide can make the disagreement smaller.
roots.sentence: Projection is the closest honest shadow an allowed space can keep.
roots.gesture: Drop one hand straight onto an imagined tabletop, forming a right angle with the discarded height.

roots.name: Singular Value Decomposition
roots.title: Singular Value Decomposition — The Important Directions of Any Matrix
roots.question: Which coordinated channels carry most of this entire transformation?
roots.object: a rectangular brass organ with input grooves and output bells
roots.failure_image: Polishing the largest rivets changes little; the loudest bell is driven by a pattern spread across many modest parts.
roots.transformation: Rotate the input wheel until each independent push rings one output direction, then order the bells from strongest to faintest.
roots.sentence: SVD separates any matrix into its strongest input-to-output channels.
roots.gesture: Turn two imaginary wheels, then lower your hands from the loudest channel to the quietest.

realms.name: The River of Change
realms.question: How does something approach, change, bend, accumulate, and reveal hidden rhythm?
realms.threshold: Beyond the chamber, the floor becomes a river. Nothing here stays still: distances shrink, slopes turn, water gathers, and tangled waves carry melodies no single moment can reveal.
realms.sound: approaching footsteps, running water, and a buried chord
realms.path: approach → local change → coupled change → bending → nearby prediction → accumulation → hidden rhythm

roots.name: Limits
roots.title: Limits — Approaching What Cannot Be Reached in One Step
roots.question: What must ‘closer and closer’ promise before we can build calculus upon it?
roots.object: stepping stones approaching a sealed luminous door
roots.failure_image: The words ‘very close’ move whenever the observer changes standards; no finite final step explains the destination.
roots.transformation: Place any tiny ring around the door. Find a stage after which every remaining stone lies inside that ring, however small the ring was chosen.
roots.sentence: A limit is a promise that every demanded closeness eventually becomes permanent.
roots.gesture: Make a shrinking circle with your fingers, then point beyond an imagined threshold.

roots.name: Partial Derivatives and Gradients
roots.title: Partial Derivatives and Gradients — One Landscape, Many Directions
roots.question: If every weight can move, which combined direction changes the loss fastest?
roots.object: a compass resting on a many-dimensional hillside
roots.failure_image: Separate one-weight trails cover the hill, but they never reveal what happens when several weights move together.
roots.transformation: Gather every coordinate slope into one arrow. The compass turns until it points toward the steepest local rise; reverse it to descend.
roots.sentence: A gradient is the compass of fastest local change.
roots.gesture: Turn an imaginary compass, then step in the opposite direction to reduce the loss.

roots.name: Jacobians
roots.title: Jacobians — When Many Outputs Change Together
roots.question: How does every output respond when every input is allowed to move?
roots.object: a wall of levers facing a wall of bells
roots.failure_image: A single slope follows one lever to one bell while the cross-effects among the rest remain invisible.
roots.transformation: Pull each lever slightly and record every bell's response in one rectangular ledger: output rows, input columns.
roots.sentence: A Jacobian is a ledger of every output's local sensitivity to every input.
roots.gesture: Fan the fingers of one hand as inputs and the other as outputs; imagine a thread between every pair.

roots.name: Hessians and Curvature
roots.title: Hessians and Curvature — Why the Same Slope Can Hide Different Valleys
roots.question: Two places have the same slope—why does one permit a bold step while the other punishes it?
roots.object: two clay valleys and a pair of rolling marbles
roots.failure_image: Both compasses show the same slope, yet one valley bends gently and the other turns into a narrow wall.
roots.transformation: Press a curvature grid into the clay. It records how each component of the gradient changes as every direction moves.
roots.sentence: A Hessian is a map of how the slope itself bends.
roots.gesture: Curve one palm like a shallow bowl and the other like a narrow valley.

roots.name: Taylor Approximation
roots.title: Taylor Approximation — Borrowing a Function’s Local Shape
roots.question: How much nearby terrain can be rebuilt from clues gathered at one point?
roots.object: a torn map, a tangent ruler, and nested pieces of curved parchment
roots.failure_image: The straight tangent predicts well for one step, then walks directly away from the bending road.
roots.transformation: Begin with the current height, add the slope's straight correction, then add curvature and finer corrections only as distance makes them necessary.
roots.sentence: A Taylor approximation rebuilds nearby shape from value, slope, curvature, and finer local clues.
roots.gesture: Lay one flat hand as a tangent, then gradually bend the other around it.

roots.name: Integrals
roots.title: Integrals — Reconstructing a Whole from Infinitesimal Pieces
roots.question: How can a changing rate become the total water actually delivered?
roots.object: a river gauge and thousands of increasingly thin glass cups
roots.failure_image: One noon reading is multiplied across the whole day, granting dawn and dusk a rate they never had.
roots.transformation: Let each tiny interval fill its own cup at its own rate, add the cups, and make them thinner until coarse partition error disappears.
roots.sentence: An integral rebuilds a whole by accumulating locally honest pieces.
roots.gesture: Cup both hands repeatedly, then gather the imagined pieces into one vessel.

roots.name: Fourier Analysis
roots.title: Fourier Analysis — Hearing Frequencies Hidden Inside Time
roots.question: Which simple rhythms are hidden inside this tangled signal?
roots.object: a dark prism surrounded by rotating tuning forks
roots.failure_image: The waveform is inspected moment by moment; overlapping notes remain one jagged line.
roots.transformation: Turn a candidate rhythm against the signal. Matching rises and falls reinforce across time while mismatched turns cancel.
roots.sentence: Fourier analysis is a prism that separates hidden rhythms.
roots.gesture: Rotate one finger in a circle while the other traces a wave.

realms.name: The Observatory of Possible Worlds
realms.question: How can uncertain possibilities become quantities, beliefs, summaries, and evidence?
realms.threshold: The river empties beneath a glass dome. Each lantern shows a different possible tomorrow; none may be extinguished merely because we do not yet know which world is real.
realms.sound: turning lenses, weighted chains, and many quiet witnesses
realms.path: possible worlds → evidence → centre and spread → settling averages → bell-shaped error → convincing claims

roots.name: Random Variables and Distributions
roots.title: Random Variables and Distributions — Turning Outcomes into Quantities
roots.question: How can stories about possible tomorrows become quantities we can calculate with?
roots.object: possible-world cards passing through a numbered brass sieve
roots.failure_image: Names such as ‘empty photograph’ and ‘two tigers’ are added as though stories were already numbers.
roots.transformation: Ask one numerical question of every world. Let different stories fall into the same numbered bowl when they give the same answer.
roots.sentence: A random variable is a numerical question asked of every possible world.
roots.gesture: Hold several imagined cards, then sort them into numbered bowls.

roots.name: Conditional Probability and Bayes’ Rule
roots.title: Conditional Probability and Bayes’ Rule — Let Evidence Rearrange Belief
roots.question: How should one paw print rearrange the brightness of competing hidden stories?
roots.object: a ring of lanterns and one fresh track beneath a lens
roots.failure_image: The brightest explanation of the print wins even if it was almost impossible before the print appeared.
roots.transformation: Begin with each lantern's old brightness, scale it by how naturally that world makes the track, then renormalize the surviving light.
roots.sentence: Bayes' rule lets evidence rearrange belief without erasing what was believed before.
roots.gesture: Dim and brighten imaginary lanterns while keeping their total light fixed.

roots.name: Expectation, Variance, and Covariance
roots.title: Expectation, Variance, and Covariance — Centre, Spread, and Shared Motion
roots.question: Where does uncertainty balance, how widely does it wander, and what moves together?
roots.object: a hanging flock-mobile with a central spindle and paired threads
roots.failure_image: Two flocks balance at the same centre, yet one is tightly gathered and the other spans the room; the mean calls them identical.
roots.transformation: Mark the balance point, measure squared wingbeats away from it, then tie paired departures together to see whether they turn in concert.
roots.sentence: Expectation finds the centre, variance the spread, and covariance the shared motion of uncertainty.
roots.gesture: Balance one palm, spread both hands apart, then move them together or oppositely.

roots.name: The Law of Large Numbers
roots.title: The Law of Large Numbers — Why Averages Eventually Settle
roots.question: Why should many imperfect witnesses reveal a stable average?
roots.object: a long procession of witnesses dropping stones onto a balance
roots.failure_image: The first witness places one stone on one side and the station declares the population average to be an extreme.
roots.transformation: Let every new witness contribute one stone, but divide by the growing crowd so headcount alone cannot inflate the answer.
roots.sentence: The law of large numbers says many honest witnesses make an average settle.
roots.gesture: Tap alternating fingers like arriving witnesses, then flatten your hand into a level balance.

roots.name: The Central Limit Theorem
roots.title: The Central Limit Theorem — Why Bell Shapes Keep Appearing
roots.question: What shape does the remaining error of a large average tend to take?
roots.object: many transparent error sheets accumulating beneath a bell-shaped canopy
roots.failure_image: The average is assumed to keep the strange shape of one individual disturbance, despite combining a hundred of them.
roots.transformation: Repeat the entire averaging experiment, centre each error, and measure it in its natural shrinking units. The stacked silhouettes smooth toward a bell.
roots.sentence: The central limit theorem gives normalized averaging error a familiar bell-shaped destination.
roots.gesture: Stack imaginary transparent sheets, then trace a bell curve over their combined outline.

roots.name: Hypothesis Tests and Confidence Intervals
roots.title: Hypothesis Tests and Confidence Intervals — When Is an Improvement Convincing?
roots.question: Is the new model's small victory a signal or an ordinary tremor of chance?
roots.object: a distant tower bell beside a brass wind-and-noise meter
roots.failure_image: One faint positive sound is celebrated without asking how loudly the empty night usually rattles the tower.
roots.transformation: Subtract the no-improvement claim and measure the remaining sound in units of ordinary sample-mean wobble; keep an interval, not only a verdict.
roots.sentence: A statistical test asks how large a signal is compared with the noise that could imitate it.
roots.gesture: Cup one ear for the signal while the other hand marks the surrounding noise.

realms.name: The Garden of Futures
realms.question: How can the present remember enough, choose well, and preserve truth inside a finite machine?
realms.threshold: A final door opens outdoors beneath a night sky. Paths branch through a garden of possible futures, cross a single bowl-shaped valley, and end at a small machine whose range is finite.
realms.sound: footsteps at crossroads, a taut string, and a machine breathing safely
realms.path: sufficient present → remembered futures → trustworthy landscape → safe computation

roots.name: Markov Chains
roots.title: Markov Chains — When the Present Carries the Relevant Past
roots.question: When can the present safely replace the entire remembered past?
roots.object: a traveler's satchel beside an impossibly long scroll of footprints
roots.failure_image: The ranger drags every footprint ever made, yet the next turn only needs information that could have been packed into today's state.
roots.transformation: Put location, weather, and every genuinely predictive fact into the present satchel. Test whether older footprints change tomorrow once the satchel is known.
roots.sentence: A Markov state is a present that carries all the past the next step still needs.
roots.gesture: Sweep an imaginary history behind you into a small satchel held at your chest.

roots.name: Dynamic Programming
roots.title: Dynamic Programming — Remembering the Value of Futures Already Solved
roots.question: How can a future already solved stop being recomputed along every road?
roots.object: a branching garden whose shared crossroads carry carved value stones
roots.failure_image: Every route redraws the same journey from the bridge to home, and the tree of copies swallows the garden.
roots.transformation: Solve the bridge once and carve its remaining value into the stone. Every upstream path may now reuse that future.
roots.sentence: Dynamic programming remembers the value of futures already solved.
roots.gesture: Trace two branching paths that meet, then tap the shared meeting point only once.

roots.name: Convexity
roots.title: Convexity — A Landscape Without Hidden Valleys
roots.question: When can a nearby valley be trusted as the lowest valley anywhere?
roots.object: a taut golden string stretched above a single clay bowl
roots.failure_image: On a rippled floor, the traveler settles in a shallow pocket while a deeper valley hides beyond a ridge.
roots.transformation: Stretch the string between any two points. If the landscape always remains below its chord, no hidden ridge can protect a better local valley.
roots.sentence: Convexity is the promise that a landscape contains no secret lower valley.
roots.gesture: Curve one palm into a bowl and stretch one finger of the other hand across it like a chord.

roots.name: Numerical Stability
roots.title: Numerical Stability — Preserving Mathematics Inside a Finite Machine
roots.question: How can a finite machine travel to the same mathematical truth without overflowing on the way?
roots.object: a small brass instrument facing three unbearably bright exponential flames
roots.failure_image: The first flame becomes infinity before the machine can compare it with the others; a meaningful ratio collapses into infinity divided by infinity.
roots.transformation: Transpose every score by the largest one. The flames shrink into the instrument's range while their relative brightness remains unchanged; restore the removed scale only at the end.
roots.sentence: Numerical stability is a safer computational path to the same mathematical truth.
roots.gesture: Lower both hands together without changing the distance between them, then raise the shared scale at the end.
